evidence_set: For cannabis, sedatives, cocaine/other stimulants and opioids, respondents reporting at least monthly use were asked additional drug-problem questions (pp.428-429). Abuse was operationalized as either of two symptoms, and dependence as at least two of four symptoms. The authors explicitly say the dependence measure did not provide formal DSM-IV criteria; the described drug-problem operationalization uses modified criteria. Lifetime alcohol dependence, in contrast, was assessed using full DSM-IV criteria (p.429). The authors explicitly acknowledge lacking ages at progression to more frequent use or onset of problems (p.431, Comment, second paragraph continuing p.432). Consequently, the lifetime drug-problem/alcohol-dependence comparisons do not by themselves establish the timing of problem onset relative to early cannabis initiation (editorial inference); order of drug initiation was separately considered. The paper's described control variables include conduct disorder, major depression, a nondiagnostic social-anxiety measure, early tobacco use and early regular alcohol use. Peer affiliation and temperament are not described as measured covariates in this paper (editorial reading of this report, not evidence that the broader register never measured them). Under Subsidiary Analyses, the authors report separate monozygotic and dizygotic analyses using early-use cutoffs before ages 15, 16 and 18, stating that they confirmed the previous conclusions; no numerical estimates for these separate analyses are printed (p.431).

Lifetime Drug Abuse/Dependence, p.428 right column bottom continuing p.429 left column; Lifetime Alcohol Dependence, p.429 left column bottom; Family, Social, and Individual Factors and Statistical Analyses, p.429 middle/right columns; Subsidiary Analyses, p.431 left column bottom continuing middle column top; Comment second paragraph beginning p.431 right column and continuing p.432 left column.
